sections.text: Thus he who does not help the revolving wheel of sacrifice, but instead leads a sinful life, rejoicing in the gratification of his senses, O Arjuna, he breathes in vain.
On the other hand, the soul who meditates on the Self is content to serve the Self and rests satisfied within the Self; there remains nothing more for him to accomplish.
He has nothing to gain by the performance or non-performance of action. His welfare depends not on any contribution that an earthly creature can make.

So we are now discussing Chapter 3, Karma Yoga, Yoga of Action. We have seen so far that Bhagavan says: Sa Yagnaha Prajaha Srushtva Pura Uvacha Prajapati Anena Prasavishyadhvam Esha Vah Twishtakamadhu. In the beginning, when Prajapati created beings (Praja), he also created Yajna.
So we are right now concerned about Praja. Praja means human beings. So the Lord of Praja is Prajapati.
The one who propagates progeny is Prajapati. So from that perspective all parents are Prajapati. So we are Prajapati for our Praja, for our children.
So what we do for our children is not that we have given them life or created their existence, but we also have to create sustenance for them. So what we do is we give them education. Then say this education will be your milch cow.
Use this education to get whatever you want. Prajapati is mentioned in Hiranya Gharba Sukta in Dhruva. So the Rig Veda says that previously there was nothing but Hiranyagarbha.
So Hiranya Garbha is something like the condition before the Big Bang. All the potentiality but no reality. So there is a singularity or the potentiality but no reality.
So that Hiranya Garbha then out of its own potential, its own creative urgent, creates a mind. This is also mentioned in Brihadaranya Upanishad and Chandogya Upanishad. Brihadaranyak Upanishad describes this Hirinyagarba.
Thus he says, first there was nothing but death and hunger. So death means nothingness. There is nothing, there is nothing to devour, nothing to enjoy by senses, because there are no senses, there is nothing.
And then he creates mind out of his creative force. And with that mind he creates water. And then water create a fire, then whatever in the water solidifies and becomes earth.
So basically the creation is explained from the beginning, when there was no creation from the no creation to creation and then a being is born in that and thats it. That being said let this body of mine be fit for a sacrifice. So thats the creation of your prajapati.
In our modern day scriptures we say brahma is the prajapati. Brahma is the creator is the prajapati. But here prajapati is very defined as the pati of praja the beings.
See in our puranas we also have daksha prajapati. He is lord of all beings. In daksha his father in law was a prajapati.
So there are several versions of this word prajapati but basically here in this case it means the primordial being from which the praja came. And then obviously that being was also concerned about how this praja will prosper. For any family man, his goal is to expand his family.
So it actually says Anena Prasavishyadhvam -- may you propagate your progeny through this. May you multiply with this. We also can take it as may you grow with this.
And then he said that this yajna which I have created is your milchka the sacrifice. That which I have created is the giver of all that you desire, all that you need. Thats what Bhagavan started in saying.
Sacrifice was created, Spirit of sacrifice was created at the same time the praja was created. The praja can only sustain itself by sacrifice. That basically was the intention of that verse.
And it almost seems like the whole idea comes from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. The same idea is also in the Kathopanishad. So basically there is a being who is the first created being.
This will be similar to the christian theory of Adam being the first man. It says that ishtakamadhu for you this will be your milchka, the sacrifice. The spirit of sacrifice will be all that you need.
And then from that you can get anything that you want. The Upanishad also says Prajapati has two types of sons: one are the Devas and the other Asuras. Now, even if we dont get into our Puranic and Vedic theories of Devas and Asuras, at our micro level the Devas are our senses.
If I take care of my senses, my senses will take care of me. If I take care of my eyes, I will take care of my world of seeing. If I take care of my ears, my ears will take care of my world of sound.
My world will be taken care of if I take care of my senses. So he said that you nourish the Devas and Devas will nourish you. At a global level or universal, we can say devas are the phenomenal forces, the nature.
If I cherish nature, nature will cherish me. And probably it was difficult to understand this concept 100 years ago. But in todays time, with the global warming and all the concern about climate change, we can understand that if we as human beings dont take care of the climate, the environment, the environment will not be able to support us as a species on this planet.
The Bhagavan said that you nourish Devas and Devas will nourish you. With that cooperative relationship, thou shall prosper. Yagna sista asinah santah muchante sarvakilbishaihi.
The good people, the righteous one, they eat the remnants of the Yajna. And by eating the remnants of the yajna they are freed from all sins. So as we have seen, the idea is not to just take whatever is left over from Yajna, but rather that the product, the profit which we make out of our cooperative endeavor -- if I share only the portion which comes rightfully to me, then I dont have a guilty feeling.
If I run a company, theres a profit. If I become so greedy that nobody else gets their share, everybody suffers. As we have seen earlier, if you get the lions share of what comes out of the collective activity -- everybody has put their sacrifice in it, they put their efforts in it -- what came out of that activity should be shared.
If I take away lions share, then Im a thief. But if I take what is rightfully mine, what comes to me as prasad from that activity, there will not be any guilt feeling. What I take from this community, I give it back.
I live in Hendricko County. I use their services, I pay my taxes. You have no guilt feeling.
If youre not paying your taxes, you will have guilt feeling. The good people who eat the remnants of Yajna, the rightful portion which comes to them as prasad of the Yajna, they are freed from all sin. They have no bondage of actions.
As we have seen, the actions have this chain reaction of cause and effect. They will not be binding to those who work in the spirit of Yajna and only take what is rightfully theirs. At the end of that endeavor, bhunja tete twadam papa e Pachanti atma karana.
The same idea is now described from the other side. One who is only acting for himself, who wants his action to benefit him alone -- that one who is cooking for himself, Pachanti, one who digests only for himself. In other words, one who only works for himself and does not want anyone else to get the benefit of his actions -- he is Pachanti Atmakarana.
Such a person is eating sins. In other words, he will have guilty feeling. No matter how much you avoid letting other people know what you are doing, your mind will constantly tell you that what you are doing is very selfish -- that you are not taking care of anyone.
If all people around me are suffering and I am enjoying just the comforts which are available to me, then Im basically living in guilt. So those who are only acting for themselves and not thinking about the rest of the community, the universe of which they are a part -- they eat sin. Because we are not islands by ourselves in this universe.
I exist because the universe exists, and we are all connected with each other. Now, that idea is very clearly demonstrated by Bhagavan in the next two verses -- that there is no separate existence for anything in this world. Everything is connected with each other.
Everything is dependent for its own existence on something else. It starts with us, the beings. These are two very famous verses.
He said Annad Bhavati Bhutani. This is the most obvious thing Bhagavan can state. Thats something you and I can vouch for that my body is made up of nothing but food.
So the beings are nothing but modification of food. Any being, any entity which is an animate entity you can think of is nothing but modification of food when it comes to the gross expression of that being. So Annad Bhavati Bhutani the beings are created from food.
The food supports the existence of being. Very obvious to all of us. No real argument here.
Parjanyat Anna Sambhavah. And this food is only possible because of rains. Us that even people who are non-vegetarian, who are eating meat -- the meat also comes from nothing but food eaten by those animals, the vegetables or whatever grows out of the ground.
So they used to say non-vegetarians are two-steps-removed vegetarians. Bhagavan said that food is only possible because the rain is coming down. And therefore we are afraid of drought.
If there is a drought, there will be famine. There wont be anything to eat. And then people will eventually die.
All beings will die because there is no food. Food is the basic ingredient which makes people in existence. And rains are possible because of collective actions.
Now, obviously this concept was difficult, as I said, for people probably who did not have this climate change. But now we can understand the rains. The climate which is supporting this cycle, eco cycle is basically dependent on the overall actions of all beings on this planet and elsewhere.
Probably also in our Vedic tradition, there is no rain. They will do some kind of Yajna to invoke the rain Gods. Even today people have experimented.
But even if we keep that aside, our actions will keep this natural balance in the environment, so that the production of food becomes regular and our existence becomes possible. Yajnaha Karma Samud Bhavaha. So the Yajna, the cooperative actions of all beings in harmony with nature, will create rains.
But this cooperative action is possible because individual actions, Karma Samudbhavam that obviously we understand, unless each one of us do our part, there wont be a cooperative action. There wont be Yajna. There is no communal projects.
So when you do communal project, the unit is an individual action. Karma Brahma Udbhavam. Now this is where I think it gets slightly complicated, as various translators have translated it very differently. At least this Bhagavad Gyasik, this Brahma is Brahma, the Creator.
The Karma is possible because Brahma has created this universe. The other translation I have seen which says Veda Karma is possible because of Veda. In other words, Veda instructs you how to act in this world.
So we can go back to that ritualism. Veda says what Karma Kant to perform. And you are now performing Karma according to that Karma Kant.
And therefore this Yajna is possible. Thats one definition. Or you can also look at it as this universe which is considered as the Brahmas creation that makes the individual action possible.
Without that, there is no individual action. So its a Karma Brahma Udbhavam with the know that Brahma Aksala Samudbhavam and that Veda or that Brahma is possible because of that imperishable Brahman, that imperishable self, then uncaused cause of all things, then imperishable Brahman is the root substratum for all that is happening. Tasmat Sarvagatam, Brahmanityam, Yagni, Pratishtama.
Therefore that all pervading self is always present in any action, in any Yajna. Without that all pervading self, none of this was possible.

These verses present a striking contrast between two ways of living. One who does not participate in the revolving wheel of Yajna, who lives only for sensory gratification (indriyarama), is said to live in vain (mogham jivati). The word mogham is powerful - it means wasteful, futile, purposeless. But the one who meditates on the Self, who is content within (atma-triptah) and satisfied by the Self alone (atmanyeva santushta), has nothing left to accomplish. For such a person, neither action nor inaction has any personal motive.
This teaching invites us to examine the purpose behind our daily activities. Are we running on the hamster wheel of sensory pleasures - seeking the next meal, the next entertainment, the next acquisition - or are we contributing to the cosmic wheel of mutual nourishment? The indriayarama (one who delights in the senses) may appear successful by worldly standards, but Krishna declares such a life to be aghayu - sinful or unwholesome.
Today, observe your activities through this lens. At the end of the day, ask yourself: How many of my actions today contributed to the cosmic wheel of Yajna? How many were purely for sensory gratification? This is not about guilt but about awareness. Then contemplate: What would it feel like to need nothing, to be atma-tripta - satisfied within myself? Even if that state seems distant, can you identify one moment today when you felt complete without needing anything external? That glimpse is your guide. Cultivate it, and the desperate pursuit of sensory pleasure will naturally diminish.
